newsitem.title: USA: White House gives upbeat assessment of NAFTA.
newsitem.headline: White House gives upbeat assessment of NAFTA.

text.p: The White House gave an upbeat assessment of the economic impact of the North American Trade Agreement in a report to be released on Friday.

The report to Congress on the first three years of NAFTA said two-way U.S. trade with Canada and Mexico had grown 44 percent since the agreement was put into effect in January 1994. Mexico and Canada also accounted for about 53 percent of the growth in total U.S. exports during the first four months of 1997, the report said.

The trade pact linking Canada, the United States and Mexico has come under heavy criticism from labor groups and some conservatives, who argue that it has meant job losses and lower wages for American workers and has done little to help improve wages and living standards for Mexican workers.

But the administration's report to Congress said the trade agreement has benefited the U.S. economy, created export jobs and helped U.S. industries -- particularly automobiles, chemicals, textiles and electronics -- become more competitive globally.

"NAFTA is permitting American companies to achieve synergies across the North American market, improving their strategic positions abroad and contributing to strong growth in employment, production and investments at home," a summary of the report released early said.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, Commerce Secretary William Daley and presidential counselor Mack McLarty, who handles Latin American affairs, were scheduled to hold a news conference on Friday morning to release the report.

Administration officials are hoping that the report will help prepare the groundwork for a push later this year for new trade negotiation authority. President Bill Clinton plans to submit proposed legislation for so-called fast-track trade negotiation authority in September.

Fast-track authority would allow administration officials to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile and undertake other market-opening trade negotiations without fear the agreements will later be changed by Congress.

The report acknowledged it was difficult to assess NAFTA's effects on the economy since it had been in place for only three years. The economic crisis in Mexico caused by the collapse of the peso in 1995-96 also makes it hard to assess the full economic impact of the trade agreement, it said.
The report cited other studies that showed modest increases in U.S. exports under the agreement.
The report emphasized Mexico's reductions in tariffs, which averaged 10 percent before NAFTA went into effect. At that time, U.S. tariffs on Mexican goods averaged a little more than 2 percent.

"Since NAFTA was signed, Mexico has reduced its average applied tariffs on U.S. imports by 7.1 percentage points, compared with a reduction of 1.4 percentage points in the United States," the report said.
The report also said the trade agreement helped Mexico recover from its financial crises quickly, a point made repeatedly by administration officials.

"In 1995, Mexico continued to implement its NAFTA obligations even as it raised tariffs on imports from other countries," the report said. "As a result, American exports recovered in 18 months and were up nearly 37 percent by the end of 1996 relative to pre-NAFTA levels, even though Mexican consumption was down 3.3 percent."
